problem: Embodied navigation (ObjectNav, multi-object finding such as MultiON/GOAT, LLM zero-shot agents) assumes static graphs with stationary targets, but household portable objects (phones, mugs, wallets) are moved by humans during the episode. Distance-to-goal rewards (DD-PPO, OVRL-V2) become high-variance with moving targets. Prior uncertain object search (Rudra et al.) only reshuffles objects between episodes and never models object transit within an episode.
motivation: Human object placement follows habits (cognitive offloading), so object movement is structured but has varying entropy: phones roam across rooms while toothbrushes or dumbbells stay in a few. An assistant robot that learns these routines could find objects in unexpected places, such as a toothbrush in a lab, and so give personalized help. Existing agents instead either chase the moving target greedily or rely on static commonsense priors.
key_idea: Make RL and LLM navigation policies 'transit-aware' (TAP) so they learn to intercept object routes rather than chase targets, and evaluate them on Dynamic Object Maps: MP3D topological graphs whose node attributes (portable objects) move along habit-structured routes.
insight: The distance-to-goal reward and greedy target chasing break down with moving targets. DD-PPO's average SR drops from 61.8 (static) to 22.4 on DOMs (RCS -63.7), and even the greedy privileged Oracle falls from 90.2 to 69.8. Replacing the distance penalty with a sparse interception reward (being on a node an object visited in the last 5 steps) keeps TAP-RL near its static performance (59.1 static vs 56.0 DOM, RCS -5.2). However, the ablation shows TAP-RL's gains depend heavily on a global per-node snapshot of object locations: with only adjacent-node counts, SR collapses to 12.6–14.3. The vanilla LLM's apparent DOM gains come from 'camping' at hub nodes shared by many object routes (Fully-Routine: SR RCS +16.7 but TA RCS -10.8). Rolling memory lets TAP-LLM exploit routine paths and find non-commonsense targets, e.g. real-lab routine SR 57.5→80.0.
method: Dynamic Object Maps (DOMs): node-attributed topological graphs built from MP3D scans. 21 portable objects (room→object mapping generated with GPT-3.5) move along precomputed shortest-path trajectories to sampled destination nodes, dwelling there 2–3 timesteps. Edges are fixed; attributes change per timestep and are stored as a nested dict {t: {node: [objects]}}.

Transit scenarios Λ with decreasing entropy: Random (any node, seed = episode index), Semi-Routine (only plausible rooms, seed = episode), Fully-Routine (plausible rooms, fixed seed s=1, so routes are identical every episode). A Static baseline has stationary objects; all objects share the same Λ.

Multi-object finding task and metrics: maximize the number of distinct portable objects found within T=30 steps from start node r. Optimal paths are computed by brute force. SR = found / max findable by the optimal policy; TA = max overlap of the agent trajectory with any optimal path; RCS (from CLIP-Nav) = relative change from static to DOM performance, where closer to 0 is better.

TAP-RL: PPO (stable-baselines3 defaults) with a masked action space (the whole graph, masked to neighbor nodes). Observation = per-node count vector of target objects over the entire graph + current node + timestep. The distance penalty is replaced by a sparse interception reward R_I = Σ_o 1[v_c ∈ P_o], triggered when an object was at the node within the last 5 steps, plus a finding reward R_f.

TAP-LLM: built on LGX. YOLO-v8 detections at the node, plus any portable objects present, form an object list. GPT-4o (appendix says GPT-4) is asked which object to go towards, and the answer is mapped to an adjacent node. The system prompt is augmented with a rolling memory of (timestep, action sequence, observed objects), truncated FIFO to avoid token overflow; in the real-world study the memory carries across episodes.

Real-to-sim pipeline: capture images of a lab at different times of day over 10 nodes and use YOLO detections as node attributes. Paste portable-object images to enrich views, DOMify with 4 targets (white mug, laptop, black remote, toothbrush; the last two are non-commonsense), then run LLM vs TAP-LLM for 50 episodes.

setting.backbone: TAP-RL: PPO policy (stable-baselines3 default architecture, trained from scratch); TAP-LLM: GPT-4o (frozen, via LGX) + YOLO-v8 detector
setting.training_data: TAP-RL: PPO trained on simulated DOM episodes over MP3D topological graphs (object trajectories generated from a GPT-3.5 room→object mapping; train/test scan split not specified). TAP-LLM: none (training-free, in-context memory only).
setting.observation: Graph-level. TAP-RL: current node, timestep, and global per-node counts of portable targets. TAP-LLM: YOLO-v8 object labels from MP3D panoramas (or real lab images) at the current node, plus portable objects present there, plus a text memory of past steps.
setting.action_space: discrete selection of a neighboring node on a topological graph (masked action space)
setting.simulator: custom DOM environment on Matterport3D topological graphs (10 scans); real-to-sim graph built from real lab images
setting.privileged: TAP-RL gets a snapshot of all portable-object locations (per-node counts over the whole graph) at every timestep and a known graph. TAP-LLM gets ground-truth presence of portable objects at the current node injected into its object list. SR is normalized by brute-force optimal paths computed with full knowledge.

numbers_note: The headline '+21.1% SR' and '+44.5% RCS' are averages of absolute point differences between TAP and non-TAP counterparts computed from the DOM table (Avg columns); they are not separate table entries. The '18.3%' real-world gain is the mean of the three per-scenario differences. Cumulative Success Rate curves, toothbrush-specific success and Time-To-Find are reported only in figures (no numbers). The Fig. caption mentions results on '5 diverse environments' but only one lab table is given. The real-world numbers come from simulated runs on a graph built from real lab images, not physical navigation.
results: On MP3D DOMs, TAP-RL reaches 56.0 average SR vs 22.4 for DD-PPO (RCS -5.2 vs -63.7), and TAP-LLM reaches 50.2 vs 41.6 for the vanilla LGX LLM (RCS -0.9 vs +31.4). The paper summarizes this as +21.1 SR and 44.5 points better RCS. In the real-lab real-to-sim study, TAP-LLM improves SR over the vanilla LLM on Random/Semi-Routine/Routine from 37.5/45.0/57.5 to 50.0/65.0/80.0, and qualitatively finds the out-of-place toothbrush more reliably. Note that a Random-walk agent (59.1 average DOM SR) and the greedy Oracle (69.8) still exceed both TAP agents in absolute DOM SR.
limitations: TAP-RL relies on privileged global observation of all object locations at every step. With only adjacent-node counts, SR collapses to about 13%. TAP-RL also changes both the observation and the reward relative to DD-PPO, so the two effects are confounded.

Highly abstract, small evaluation: graph-level navigation on 10 MP3D scans with 30-step episodes and symbolic portable objects (no perception of moved objects), and the same Λ for all objects. A random agent beats both TAP agents in absolute average DOM SR, and RCS rewards consistency rather than absolute performance.

The 'real-world' study is a single 10-node lab graph with 4 objects evaluated via real-to-sim simulated runs rather than quantified physical robot navigation. The GPT-4 vs GPT-4o descriptions are inconsistent, and code/data were not yet released.
